tip: After 'è bello che' (it's nice that), the verb goes subjunctive: 'siate', not 'siete'.
Descriptive adjectives usually follow the noun: 'vestiti nuovi' = new clothes, literally clothes new.
Verbs ending '-gare' add an h before i to keep the hard g: 'navigare' gives 'navighi' = you browse.
Verbs in '-giare' keep a single i for 'tu': 'assaggiare' becomes 'assaggi' = you taste, never 'assaggii'.
'Provare' links to a following verb with 'a', not 'di': 'prova a capire' = she tries to understand.
The article, not the word ending, is the real gender signal. 'La pasta' is feminine, so its adjective agrees: 'pronta', both ending in '-a'.
'Controllare' usually means to check, not to control: 'controlli il calendario' = you check the calendar.
Use 'lo', not 'il', before s plus consonant, z, or gn: 'lo spettacolo' = the show, 'lo zaino' = the backpack.
Masculine 'un' takes no apostrophe before a vowel: 'un albero' = a tree. The feminine does: 'un'amica'.
'Andare' (to go) and 'venire' (to come) are opposite – 'venire' implies coming toward the speaker.
'Acqua naturale' means still water, not natural: 'beviamo acqua naturale'. Sparkling is 'acqua frizzante'.
Meals use 'fare', not 'avere': 'fa colazione' = he has breakfast, with no article before 'colazione'.
'Sapere' is knowing facts or how to do things: 'sai la risposta' = you know the answer. For people or places use 'conoscere'.
'Volere' is irregular: 'voglio, vuoi, vuole, vogliamo, volete, vogliono'; 'lui vuole' = he wants.
Age uses 'avere', not to be: 'ho ventitré anni' = I am twenty-three, literally I have twenty-three years.
Weather uses 'fare': 'fa caldo' = it is hot, 'fa freddo' = it is cold, literally it makes heat.
'Tenere' is irregular: 'tengo', 'tieni', 'lui tiene' = he holds. The stressed e becomes ie.
'Di più' means more and comes after the verb: 'riposare di più' = rest more, never 'più riposare'.
Being right uses 'avere': 'hai ragione' = you are right, literally you have reason. The opposite is 'avere torto'.
The adjective matches the noun's gender: 'la neve è bianca' (f), but 'il muro è bianco' (m).
'Stare' covers how you are right now: 'non stai attento' = you're not paying attention. Current states take 'stare', not 'essere'.
A yes/no question keeps statement word order: 'puoi ripetere' means you can repeat, turned into a question just by rising intonation.
The progressive is 'stare' plus an '-ndo' form: 'sta cucinando' = he is cooking right now.
'In ritardo' means late or delayed, and the preposition is always 'in': 'il treno arriva in ritardo'.
Months usually take 'a': 'a settembre' = in September, 'a giugno' = in June.
'Camera' means a room or bedroom, not a photo camera (that is 'macchina fotografica'): 'la mia camera' = my room.
With a reflexive, Italian uses the article, not a possessive: 'mi lavo i denti' = I brush my teeth, literally the teeth.
'Avere ragione', literally to have reason, is how Italian says to be right: 'abbiano ragione'.
The present subjunctive of 'avere' is 'abbia', identical for 'io', 'tu', and 'lui': 'che tu abbia'.
'Soldi' (money) is always plural in Italian: 'risparmio soldi' = I save money, 'non ho soldi' = I have no money.
